Pluck means to pull something sharply and quickly — usually to remove it from where it is attached, stuck, or held. Think of it as a confident, deliberate little tug that separates something from its place.

That one core idea — a quick, purposeful pull — runs through every meaning of this word. Once you feel it, all the uses will make sense.

1. To pull something off or out of where it is attached

This is the most fundamental use. You pluck something when you grab it and pull it free in one swift motion.

  • You pluck a flower from a bush.
  • You pluck a ripe apple from a tree.
  • You pluck a grey hair from your head.
  • A surgeon plucks a splinter from a wound.

Notice the action: it's not slow and gentle, and it's not violent. It's quick, clean, and deliberate. The thing being plucked was attached somewhere, and after the action, it is free.

2. To remove feathers from a bird

This is a very specific but common use. When a chicken or duck is prepared for cooking, its feathers are pulled out one by one (or in handfuls). This is called plucking the bird.

  • The cook plucked the chicken before roasting it.

3. To pull the strings of a musical instrument

When you play a guitar, harp, or sitar, you don't press the strings down with a bow like a violin — you pull them with your finger or a pick and let go, which makes them vibrate and produce sound. That action is called plucking.

  • She plucked the strings of her harp softly.
  • He plucked a single note on his guitar.

The action is exactly the same — a quick pull-and-release — but applied to music.

4. To grab and move someone or something quickly

Here, pluck means to seize someone or something and move them rapidly — often from one situation to another, sometimes from danger to safety. The idea of a quick, decisive action is still there.

  • The lifeguard plucked the child from the water.
  • He was plucked from obscurity and made a star overnight.
  • She plucked the phone from his hand before he could answer.

Notice the slight flavour here: there's a sense of being lifted out of a situation entirely, almost like picking a flower. The person or thing was in one place, and in a moment, they are gone from it.

5. To lightly pull or tug at something (without removing it)

Sometimes you pluck at something — meaning you pull at it gently and repeatedly, but without actually removing it. This is used when someone is nervously fidgeting, or trying to get someone's attention by tugging on their clothing.

  • He nervously plucked at his collar during the interview.
  • She plucked at his sleeve to get his attention.
  • The child plucked at the loose threads on the sofa.

This use is softer and more tentative than the others — there is no firm removal happening, just a repeated gentle pull.

Pluck up is one of the most important and widely used phrases built from this word. It almost always appears in one specific phrase:

"to pluck up the courage (to do something)"

It means to gather enough bravery within yourself to do something that feels difficult or frightening. Imagine that courage is something scattered inside you, and you're pulling it all together into one place — that's the image behind this phrase.

  • He finally plucked up the courage to ask for a raise.
  • She plucked up the courage to tell him the truth.
  • I've been trying to pluck up the nerve to call her for weeks.

You will also hear "pluck up the nerve" — it means exactly the same thing. "Nerve" here is an informal word for courage.

Every single use of "pluck" as a verb shares the same underlying energy: a quick, deliberate pulling action. Whether you are:

  • pulling a petal off a flower,
  • pulling a string on a guitar,
  • pulling a child from danger,
  • or pulling courage up from inside yourself,

...the word always carries that same crisp, decisive quality. It is never slow. It is never accidental. There is always intention behind it.

Here are some naturally flowing sentences that show the full range of the word in real use, so you can feel how native speakers use it:

  • She plucked a strawberry from the bowl and popped it in her mouth.
  • The eagle plucked a fish right out of the river.
  • He sat plucking his guitar on the porch all evening.
  • The director plucked an unknown actress from a small town and made her famous.
  • She anxiously plucked at the hem of her dress as she waited.
  • I just need to pluck up the courage and go talk to him.
One Sentence to Remember It All

"Pluck" is the verb for any action where something is quickly and deliberately pulled — whether it's a hair from your head, a note from a guitar string, a person from danger, or courage from within yourself.
